A1.justification: These are identifiable revisions of the same work despite the changed title and expanded B-Tree scope. All pages, equations and figures support comparison. Both PDFs end with references; neither contains an appendix.

before.justification: v1 reports algorithmic constructions, mathematical guarantees and counterexamples. Its references to empirical outcomes concern other work; no original empirical study is reported.

after.justification: v2 likewise reports theoretical results. Figures 1–2 and the access-sequence comparison in Section 6.2 are constructed illustrations and analytical examples, not experiments or simulations.

M1.justification: The original double-logarithmic BST construction is retained using inverse-weight notation. v2 adds a B-Tree construction that partitions the Treap by priority tiers, converts the resulting subtrees into B-Treaps and reconnects them (Section 5). Section 6 develops the earlier future-working-set idea using weights 1/(1+interval)^2; the separate past-working-set scheme is no longer presented.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or empirical training/evaluation tasks. The extension to external-memory B-Trees is a theoretical model extension, not added experimental coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version reports empirical baseline evaluations. The analytical comparisons with Lin–Luo–Woodruff's priority assignment and the single-logarithm alternative are retained in v2 Section 4.4.

E3.justification: Neither PDF specifies an empirical evaluation protocol, data splits, training budgets or experimental metrics. New branching-factor conditions and prediction-error measures are assumptions in mathematical guarantees.

E4.justification: Neither version contains empirical ablations, robustness tests or observed error studies. The alternative-priority counterexamples are retained; the expanded formal prediction-error guarantees are mathematical developments assessed under T1.

E5.justification: Neither reports repeated experimental runs, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. v2's additional high-probability guarantees concern algorithmic randomness, not statistical reporting of empirical results.

E6.justification: Neither version reports measured performance values, benchmark rankings or empirical findings. v2's new asymptotic bounds and numerical entries in its worked illustration are theoretical content.

T1.justification: v2 replaces the smooth-score formulation with bounded-l1 weights and adds B-Treap static and dynamic theorems, branching-factor conditions, high-probability claims, and error bounds involving several distribution distances and absolute prediction error. It also replaces sum-of-depths update accounting with a stronger logarithmic weight-ratio claim. The interval-set definitions and proofs develop v1's future-working-set argument, while its separate past-working-set theorem is not retained.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes arbitrary-input learning-augmented BSTs attaining static optimality and working-set bounds with rough predictions. v2 retains the BST contribution but adds the central claim of the first B-Tree exploiting access-sequence locality through online reorganization, together with dynamic prediction-error guarantees.

C2.justification: v2 explains why dynamic optimality would limit the asymptotic benefit of predictions for BSTs and why temporal locality is pursued instead of spatial locality (Section 3). Its cyclic-versus-grouped sequence example also explains when dynamic B-Treaps can outperform static trees (Section 6.2). These add substantive interpretation to the retained locality and update-cost discussion.

D1.justification: v2 specifies an 11-wise independent hash function for generating uniform priority perturbations in Theorem 4.4 and Lemma 5.1; v1 only specifies uniform random draws. Neither provides implementation code, hardware information or experimental reproduction instructions.

R1.justification: v2 substantially refocuses the literature discussion around beyond-worst-case search trees and B-Trees in external memory. It adds Golovin's B-Treaps, subsequent B-Tree work, distribution-learning references and recommender-system error measures, while removing much of v1's broad ski-rental, knapsack and balanced-tree survey. The relationship to Lin–Luo–Woodruff remains central.

P1.justification: The title becomes Learning-Augmented B-Trees and the author list expands. The introduction is extensively rewritten, a standalone Overview is introduced, related work becomes Section 3, and preliminaries are incorporated into the static BST section. Repeated informal theorem statements and the standalone conclusion disappear, and score-respecting terminology becomes composite-priority terminology.

P2.justification: v1 has no numbered figures or tables. v2 adds Figure 1 illustrating static versus dynamic trees and Figure 2 illustrating interval and working-set sizes with tabulated example values. The title-page author layout also changes; the main document retains its single-column mathematical presentation.

improvement.justification: The B-Tree treatment and new overview and figures broaden the contribution and improve accessibility. However, v1 explicitly charges updates by the sum of old and new depths (Remark 1.2), whereas v2 Theorem 5.2 claims a logarithmic weight-ratio cost justified only by deleting and reinserting. That argument does not establish the stronger bound used in Section 6. Theorem 6.9 also labels an unnormalized absolute-error sum as MAE. These unresolved issues in central new guarantees prevent a reliable net-quality judgment.
